paragraphs: The people of America are now called on to decide a question whose consequences must prove among the most important that ever engaged their attention. When they reflect on this, it will be evident that they ought to take a view of it that is both very comprehensive and very serious.

Nothing is more certain than that government is indispensably necessary. It is equally undeniable that, whenever and however government is set up, the people must give up some of their natural rights to give it the powers it needs. It is therefore well worth considering which would serve the interest of the people of America better. They could be, for all general purposes, one nation under one federal government. Or they could divide themselves into separate confederacies and give the head of each the same kind of powers that they are now advised to place in one national government.

Until lately it was a received and uncontradicted opinion that the prosperity of the people of America depended on their staying firmly united, and the wishes, prayers, and efforts of our best and wisest citizens have always been directed to that goal. But politicians have now appeared who insist that this opinion is mistaken. They say that instead of looking for safety and happiness in union, we ought to seek them in dividing the States into distinct confederacies or sovereignties. However extraordinary this new doctrine may seem, it has its advocates, and some who formerly opposed it strongly are now among them. Whatever arguments or inducements have brought about this change in the views and declarations of these gentlemen, it would certainly be unwise for the people at large to adopt these new political tenets without being fully convinced that they rest on truth and sound policy.

It has often given me pleasure to observe that independent America was not made up of detached and distant territories. One connected, fertile, wide-spreading country was the portion of our western sons of liberty. Providence has blessed it in a special way with a variety of soils and products, and has watered it with countless streams for the delight and convenience of its inhabitants. A succession of navigable waters forms a kind of chain around its borders, as if to bind it together. The noblest rivers in the world, running at convenient distances, give the people highways for easily sending friendly aid to one another and for carrying and exchanging their various goods.

With equal pleasure I have as often noticed that Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people. They descend from the same ancestors, speak the same language, profess the same religion, and are attached to the same principles of government. Their manners and customs are very similar. By their joint counsels, arms, and efforts, fighting side by side through a long and bloody war, they have nobly won general liberty and independence.

This country and this people seem to have been made for each other. It appears to have been the design of Providence that an inheritance so suitable and convenient for a band of brothers, joined together by the strongest ties, should never be split into a number of unsociable, jealous, and alien sovereignties.

Similar views have until now prevailed among all ranks and denominations of men among us. For all general purposes we have always been one people, with every citizen everywhere enjoying the same national rights, privileges, and protection. As a nation we have made peace and war. As a nation we have defeated our common enemies. As a nation we have formed alliances, made treaties, and entered into various compacts and conventions with foreign states.

A strong sense of the value and blessings of union led the people, very early, to set up a federal government to preserve and perpetuate it. They formed it almost as soon as they had a political existence. They formed it even while their homes were in flames, while many of their citizens were bleeding, and while the progress of hostility and devastation left little room for the calm and mature inquiry and reflection that must always come before the formation of a wise and well-balanced government for a free people. It is no wonder that a government set up in times so unfavorable should be found, when tried, to be greatly deficient and inadequate to its purpose.

This intelligent people saw these defects and regretted them. They remained as attached to union as they were devoted to liberty. They saw that the first was in immediate danger and the second in more distant danger. They were persuaded that ample security for both could be found only in a more wisely framed national government. So, as with one voice, they convened the recent convention at Philadelphia to take that important subject under consideration.

This convention was made up of men who had the confidence of the people. Many of them had become highly distinguished for patriotism, virtue and wisdom in times that tried the minds and hearts of men. They undertook the difficult task. In the gentle season of peace, with minds free of other subjects, they spent many months in calm, uninterrupted, daily consultation. In the end, without having been overawed by power or swayed by any passion except love of country, they presented and recommended to the people the plan produced by their joint and very unanimous counsels.

Grant that this plan is only RECOMMENDED, not imposed, which is the fact. Yet remember that it is recommended neither to BLIND approval nor to BLIND rejection. It is recommended to that calm and fair consideration which the size and importance of the subject demand, and which it certainly ought to receive. But (as the preceding number remarked) it is more to be wished than expected that it will be so considered and examined. Experience on a former occasion teaches us not to be too hopeful about this. It is not yet forgotten that well-founded fears of imminent danger led the people of America to form the memorable Congress of 1774. That body recommended certain measures to its constituents, and events proved its wisdom. Yet we remember how soon the press began to swarm with pamphlets and weekly papers against those very measures. Many officers of government who obeyed the dictates of personal interest worked tirelessly to persuade the people to reject the advice of that patriotic Congress. So did others, whether from a mistaken estimate of consequences, or the undue influence of former attachments, or an ambition that aimed at objects that did not match the public good. Many were indeed deceived and misled, but the great majority of the people reasoned and decided wisely, and they are glad to reflect that they did.

They considered that the Congress was made up of many wise and experienced men. They considered that, having come together from different parts of the country, those men brought with them a variety of useful information and shared it with one another. They considered that, in the time they spent together inquiring into and discussing the true interests of their country, they must have gained very accurate knowledge of them. And they considered that those men each had a personal stake in the public liberty and prosperity, so that it was no less their inclination than their duty to recommend only such measures as, after the most mature deliberation, they really thought prudent and advisable.

These and similar considerations led the people to rely greatly on the judgment and integrity of the Congress, and they took its advice despite the various arts and efforts used to deter them. The people at large had reason to trust the men of that Congress, though few of them had been fully tested or generally known. They now have still greater reason to respect the judgment and advice of the convention. For it is well known that some of the most distinguished members of that Congress were also members of this convention. They have since been tested and rightly approved for patriotism and ability, and they have grown old in acquiring political knowledge. They carried their accumulated knowledge and experience into the convention.

It is worth remarking that not only the first Congress but every Congress since, and the recent convention as well, have always agreed with the people in thinking that the prosperity of America depended on its Union. To preserve and perpetuate it was the great object of the people in forming that convention, and it is also the great object of the plan the convention has advised them to adopt. With what propriety, then, or for what good purposes, do some men at this particular time try to belittle the importance of the Union? Or why is it suggested that three or four confederacies would be better than one? I am persuaded in my own mind that the people have always thought rightly on this subject. I am persuaded that their universal and uniform attachment to the cause of the Union rests on great and weighty reasons, which I shall endeavor to develop and explain in some of the following papers. Those who promote the idea of putting a number of distinct confederacies in the place of the convention's plan seem clearly to foresee that rejecting the plan would put the continuance of the Union in the utmost jeopardy. That certainly would be the case. I sincerely wish that every good citizen may foresee as clearly that, whenever the dissolution of the Union arrives, America will have reason to exclaim, in the words of the poet: "FAREWELL! A LONG FAREWELL TO ALL MY GREATNESS."
